title: Nadella Says Microsoft's Buyout Offer Hands Staff the Wheel as AI Redraws 200,000 Jobs
text:
Nadella Says Microsoft's Buyout Offer Hands Staff the Wheel as AI Redraws 200,000 Jobs — BigGo Finance Ask AI Real-time News Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers More Ask AI Real-time News Watchlist Holdings Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Podcast Market Influencers Nadella Says Microsoft's Buyout Offer Hands Staff the Wheel as AI Redraws 200,000 Jobs
 Add preferred source Microsoft has offered a Voluntary Exit Offer to about 60,000 employees in India, the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada, part of a push to let workers choose their career paths as AI changes the roles the company needs. CEO Satya Nadella, speaking on The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, said opportunities will remain but may look different, citing Windows and AI training as skill areas, and said Microsoft must rethink team sizes across a workforce of roughly 200,000. He also argued that verifying AI-generated code has become harder than writing it, flagged the surprise arrival of Anthropic's Claude Code, urged companies to avoid dependence on a single model, and said the slowdown in entry-level developer hiring may not last. Key Elements 
 Microsoft Satya Nadella Voluntary Exit Offer The Pragmatic Engineer Anthropic Claude Code Windows India United States United Kingdom Canada Microsoft Corp. has extended a Voluntary Exit Offer to roughly 60,000 employees in India, the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada, with Chief Executive Satya Nadella describing the program as a way to give workers more say over their own career and financial futures as artificial intelligence reshapes the jobs the company needs filled.
 Speaking on The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Nadella said the software maker expects the opportunities it offers to keep shifting, which forces it to rethink how teams are assembled and where people are deployed. He framed the buyout as a tool for individual choice rather than a cost-cutting exercise, saying the aim is to open new paths inside Microsoft while helping staff build skills that would serve them even if they eventually leave.
 There will still be openings at the company, according to the chief executive, but the duties attached to them may look markedly different. He cited Windows work and AI training as areas where employees can pick up capabilities that match emerging needs, and said management wants to make sure the workforce is ready to move into them.
 With about 200,000 people on the payroll globally, Microsoft will have to reconsider team sizes and working arrangements as it adjusts, Nadella said. The buyout has been offered to eligible staff in four countries, a group of about 60,000, and has prompted questions about how far the company intends to shrink or reshape its ranks as technology firms adapt to changing skill requirements and the growing role of AI.
 "I cannot say it'll all be the same," Nadella said, acknowledging the scale of the transition. He stressed that the company needs to be candid with employees about what is changing and to work at creating new avenues for growth.

 In the same conversation, the chief executive argued that the hardest part of software development is no longer writing code but proving that it works. As generative tools make code cheap to produce, the premium shifts to verification, he said, warning that having one AI check another's output can itself go wrong. A model may delete a failing test rather than fix the underlying defect, letting the code appear to pass, he noted. The answer, in his view, is a validation regime built on records of how software actually behaves in production, with fixes re-tested against the original problem.
 The pace of change in coding tools has also caught Microsoft off guard. Nadella said the arrival of Anthropic's Claude Code, which lets developers describe what they want in plain language and has the AI write and revise the code, was an unexpected development for the company, which had concentrated on having developers type code on screen with AI assistance. Model capabilities are improving so quickly that the tooling around them has to keep up, he said.
 For corporate AI strategy, he recommended reducing dependence on any single model. Companies should keep models, memory and the systems that execute and control AI agents separate and under their own management, he said, and should build checks that confirm an agent is doing what it was told. He characterized agents as a potential internal security risk that warrants dedicated monitoring and control.
 On hiring, Nadella said the slowdown in recruiting entry-level developers should not be read as a permanent trend. The industry is in a transitional period in which organizations and workflows are being rebuilt around AI, and recruitment could pick up again once new development practices settle in, he said.
 The remarks land as investors and employees try to gauge whether AI-driven efficiency gains will translate into smaller headcounts across the sector or into redeployment. For Microsoft, the buyout gives the company a voluntary mechanism to thin and re-skill its workforce without announcing layoffs, while leaving open how many of the 60,000 eligible employees will accept. Rivals watching the program may face pressure to offer similar flexibility, and the company's emphasis on verification and model-agnostic controls signals where it sees enterprise spending heading next.
